idiom_name: sync.RWMutex: RLock/RUnlock for readers, Lock/Unlock for the writer
implementation_notes: sync.RWMutex is the stdlib primitive: the zero value is an unlocked mutex, readers call RLock/RUnlock (shared) and the writer calls Lock/Unlock (exclusive). The implementation is deliberately writer-biased - while a writer is pending, new RLock calls block so the writer eventually gets the lock - which also means recursive read locking is a deadlock and neither read-to-write upgrade nor write-to-read downgrade exists. Prefer channels when the shared thing is really a handoff ('share memory by communicating'); use RWMutex for read-mostly maps, caches and registries, embedded as a field of the owning struct (never copied after first use) with readers dominating.
pitfalls: An RWMutex must not be copied after first use (go vet's copylocks catches the common cases); always pass the owning struct by pointer.
Recursive RLock deadlocks: a waiting Lock makes further RLock calls block, so a reader method must not call another method that takes the read lock.
RLock protects the guarded field, not everything reachable from it; handing out a map or slice during a read lets callers mutate shared state outside the lock.
Holding RLock across channel operations or long computations delays the writer arbitrarily - keep read sections bounded.
